Interface StateBehaviorContext

All Known Implementing Classes:
AnimatedAreaAnalysisCase, AnimatedAreaGeospatialAnalysisCase, BarChartAnalysisCase, BarChartsDisplay, BarGraphRendering, GraphicalRendering, HTMLDisplay, InteractionMessageSequenceDisplay, InterconnectionDiagramRendering, LineChartsAnalysisCase, NeuralNetworkAnalysisCase, ObjectiveFunctionAnalysisCase, ParametricAnalysisCase, PartContainer, RequirementsSpecRendering, ScatterPlotAnalysisCase, SysMLFlowConnector, SysMLPart, SysMLPort, SysMLRendering, SysMLStakeholder, SysMLVerificationCase, SysMLView, TabularRendering, TextualRendering, TradeOffAnalysisCase
public interface StateBehaviorContext
SysMLinJava-specific interface for model elements that exhibit state-based behavior, i.e. a part, port, or other element whose behavior is defined by an asychronous state machine. Implementation of this interface enables more precise modeling of the element for model execution. Implementing elements should implement the interface by including instances of an extended SysMLStateMachine and a ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor in their class as done by the SysMLPart and the SysMLPort.

  • Method Details

    • start

      void start()
      Starts the event-driven's state machine behavior, if a state machine is present. The operation submits an InitialEvent to the state machine's event queue to thereby start its execution thread. The state machine will execute in accordance with the states and transitions that are defined in the class that extends the SysMLStateMachine.

      Note this method is provided to enable model execution. It is not part of the SysML standard, To the extent the SysML standard does not provide elements for executable modeling per se, SysMLinJava includes various model elements to enable model execution.

      See Also:
      • SysMLPart.start()

    • acceptEvent

      void acceptEvent(SysMLEvent event)
      Accepts and queues a specified event into the state machine's event queue. Whereas the event queue is a thread safe object, this method can be called to inject an event into the state machine from any thread.

      Note this method is provided to enable model execution. It is not part of the SysML standard, To the extent the SysML standard does not provide elements for executable modeling per se, SysMLinJava includes various model elements to enable model execution.

      Parameters:
      event - event to be queued to the state machine
      See Also:
      • SysMLPart.acceptEvent(SysMLEvent)

    • stop

      void stop()
      Stops the event-driven's state machine-based behavior, if a state machine is present in the event-driven. The operation simply stops the state machine execution. Note if this event-driven's state machine is asynchronous, i.e. executes in its own thread, then this operation imposes a "hard stop" where the thread is canceled regardless of what state it's in. If the part or port's state machine is synchronous, this operation can only queue up a FinalEvent to the event queue, on the assumption that the state machine is capable of handling the FinalEvent at the point in which the stop() method is invoked. Therefore, if a event-driven is synchronous and this stop method is used, it's state machine should be modeled to handle the FinalEvent accordingly.

      Note this method is provided to enable model execution. It is not part of the SysML standard, To the extent the SysML standard does not provide elements for executable modeling per se, SysMLinJava includes various model elements to enable model execution.

      See Also:
      • SysMLPart.stop()

    • delay

      void delay(double seconds)
      Delays the calling thread (sleeps) for the specified seconds of time.

      Note this method is provided to enable model execution. It is not part of the SysML standard, To the extent the SysML standard does not provide elements for executable modeling per se, SysMLinJava includes various model elements to enable model execution.

      Parameters:
      seconds - time to sleep in seconds. Use up to 3 decimal places for fractions of a second, i.e. the delay is capable of the milliseconds precision provided by java's Thread.sleep(<millis>) operation.
      See Also:
